surveyDefinition.title: Organic Milk — consumer survey (North America)
surveyDefinition.studyPurpose: Identify which of 4 behavioural segments each respondent belongs to, based on their organic milk purchase frequency, price sensitivity, and the motivations (health, ethics, taste) that drive their choice.

segments.name: Price-Sensitive Households
segments.description: Buy organic milk regularly but are highly attentive to price, often comparing with conventional milk and switching to the cheapest organic option or reducing purchase frequency when prices rise. They buy for family health but are constrained by budget.

segments.name: Committed Organic Buyers
segments.description: Buy organic milk consistently and are willing to pay a premium without much hesitation. They are driven by strong beliefs about health, animal welfare, and environmental sustainability, and are loyal to the organic category and often to specific brands.

segments.name: Occasional Organic Buyers
segments.description: Buy organic milk infrequently, often as a treat or for a specific use (e.g., for a child, for coffee), but mostly buy conventional milk. They are not committed to organic and are easily swayed by price or availability.

segments.name: Health & Quality-Driven Buyers
segments.description: Buy organic milk primarily for perceived health and nutritional benefits, and for superior taste and quality. They are less motivated by environmental or ethical concerns and more by personal and family wellbeing. They are willing to pay a premium for quality but may not be loyal to organic per se if a better-tasting or more nutritious alternative appears.

surveyDefinition.whatThisSurveyIs: A segmentation study of Organic Milk buyers in North America. It asks how people use Organic Milk, how they choose it, and what would make them switch — then sorts respondents into the behavioural groups defined below. Questions stay at category level: no named brands, and nothing about adjacent categories.
surveyDefinition.whoseContextThisIs: Adults in North America who buy or use Organic Milk for personal or household use. Respondents qualify if they: Primary or shared grocery shopper in the household; Buys milk at least once a month; Has purchased organic milk in the past 3 months. Excluded: Institutional buyers (restaurants, cafeterias, food service); People who never buy milk or exclusively buy non-dairy alternatives.
surveyDefinition.whyTheseRespondents: Household shoppers buy organic milk, pay for it themselves, and decide at the shelf. Retailers and supermarkets sell it, but the end consumer is the individual household. There is no meaningful business-only purchase channel for organic milk.
respondentBehaviours: Purchases organic milk regularly (weekly or bi-weekly)
Reads labels for organic certification and freshness
Willing to pay a premium for perceived health and environmental benefits
May also buy other organic dairy or grocery products
whatIsDeliberatelyNotAsked: Age or household income as behavioural questions — no finding in this survey is driven by them. They are asked once, at the end, in Profiling, and used only to cross-tabulate the behavioural results.
Brand, company or manufacturer names — the survey stays at category level so findings are not tied to one competitor set.
Where the respondent lives — region is chosen when viewing the results, so asking it again would waste a question.
surveyDefinition.howToReadTheNumbers: Percentages are simulated from a persona-weighted panel of 2,500 synthetic respondents built from real market evidence, not from fieldwork. Single-choice, ranking and rating-scale questions sum to 100%. Multi-select questions do not — each option is an independent share of respondents choosing it. The N shown on each question is the display base for that item.

sections.label: Household Consumption & Usage Context
sections.covers: Establishes who drinks organic milk, how often, and in what situations, to separate daily users from occasional ones.

sections.label: Grocery Purchase Behaviour & Channel
sections.covers: Covers how and where organic milk is bought, including restock cycle, spend, and what triggers a purchase.

sections.label: Product, Provenance & Claim Requirements
sections.covers: Explores what attributes matter most, including fat content, packaging, certifications, and trade-offs against price.

sections.label: Satisfaction, Loyalty & Switching Risk
sections.covers: Measures overall satisfaction, what drives it, and what would make buyers switch away from organic milk.

structure.storyline: Questions run in a planned narrative order: broad and easy first, specific and sensitive last.
structure.storylineSummary: The survey opens by establishing the household's overall milk consumption and the role of organic within it, then moves to the purchase journey—what triggers a buy, how often, where, and what decides the choice. It then probes product expectations, including certifications and price trade-offs, and closes with satisfaction, loyalty, and switching risk. The arc moves from broad, safe questions about usage to more sensitive topics like price tolerance and switching intent, allowing the segmentation to emerge from behavioural and motivational data.

metadata.studyPurpose: Identify which of 4 behavioural segments each respondent belongs to, based on their organic milk purchase frequency, price sensitivity, and the motivations (health, ethics, taste) that drive their choice.
metadata.segmentation_lens: Price sensitivity combined with purchase motivation (jobs-to-be-done). Organic milk is a premium staple where the core behavioural difference is how much of a price premium buyers will tolerate and what job they hire the milk to do (family health, personal ethics, or taste).

segments.name: Price-Sensitive Households
segments.description: Buy organic milk regularly but are highly attentive to price, often comparing with conventional milk and switching to the cheapest organic option or reducing purchase frequency when prices rise. They buy for family health but are constrained by budget.
segments.hypothesis: This group will show high price sensitivity in trade-off questions, lower willingness to pay a premium, and a tendency to buy larger pack sizes to reduce per-unit cost.

segments.name: Committed Organic Buyers
segments.description: Buy organic milk consistently and are willing to pay a premium without much hesitation. They are driven by strong beliefs about health, animal welfare, and environmental sustainability, and are loyal to the organic category and often to specific brands.
segments.hypothesis: This group will show low price sensitivity, high importance on organic certification and ethical claims, and high loyalty and advocacy.

segments.name: Occasional Organic Buyers
segments.description: Buy organic milk infrequently, often as a treat or for a specific use (e.g., for a child, for coffee), but mostly buy conventional milk. They are not committed to organic and are easily swayed by price or availability.
segments.hypothesis: This group will show low purchase frequency, high price sensitivity, and lower importance on organic claims; they may switch back to conventional easily.

segments.name: Health & Quality-Driven Buyers
segments.description: Buy organic milk primarily for perceived health and nutritional benefits, and for superior taste and quality. They are less motivated by environmental or ethical concerns and more by personal and family wellbeing. They are willing to pay a premium for quality but may not be loyal to organic per se if a better-tasting or more nutritious alternative appears.
segments.hypothesis: This group will rate health and taste attributes highly, show moderate price sensitivity, and be less concerned with sustainability claims.

segmentModel.tie_break: Question pe6 (If the price of your usual organic milk rose by 20%, which would you most likely do?) is the most direct behavioural self-report because it forces respondents to choose between price sensitivity and commitment, cleanly separating price_sensitive_households from committed_organic_buyers and health_quality_driven_buyers.
notes: Occasional buyers are identified by low frequency (cp1, cp6) and willingness to substitute (cp5).
Price-sensitive households are identified by price comparison behaviour (bb4) and reaction to price increases (pe6, sf6).
Committed organic buyers show high frequency, loyalty, and ethical motivations (cp1, cp5, cp8, pe5, sf6).
Health & quality-driven buyers focus on taste, nutrition, and personal benefits (cp8, pe1, pe2, sf4, sf6).
6 scoring weight(s) removed: they scored questions that were dropped as duplicates before publication.
segmentModel.excluded: Screening and Profiling questions are excluded from scoring: screeners carry no signal (everyone passed) and demographics are for cross-tabs, not segmentation.

fieldingNotes.recommendedSample: n=800-1,200 for stable segment-level sub-groups (roughly n>=312 per segment after weighting). At n=1,000 the margin of error on a whole-sample percentage is about ±3.1pp at 95% confidence; on a segment of n=200 it widens to about ±6.9pp, so segment-level differences under ~10pp should not be reported as real.
fieldingNotes.quotaControls: Apply quotas on the category-usage and frequency screeners so heavy users — who are more willing survey-takers — are not over-sampled.
scriptingNotes: Rotate the order of answer options on every non-ordinal question to remove primacy bias. Do NOT rotate ordinal scales (frequency bands, price bands, satisfaction) — their order carries meaning.
Anchor 'Other', 'None of these' and 'Prefer not to say' to the bottom of the list, exempt from rotation.
Every 'Other' option takes an open-text capture, coded back into the frame at analysis if any single verbatim exceeds 3%.
No routing or skip logic: every respondent sees every question, so the base is constant across the instrument.
Include one attention check in the middle third — a standard instructed-response item. Terminate on failure and replace.
Randomise the order of the two ranking/trade-off items between respondents so neither is systematically answered while fresher.
caveats: Percentages in this document are simulated from a persona-weighted panel, not fielded with real respondents. Replace with primary data after fielding.
Ranking items are shown as a lighter-weight ranking exercise; run them as MaxDiff if you need more precision on driver importance.
Profiling questions are for cross-tabs only and are excluded from the segmentation scoring model.

metadata.storyline_summary: The survey opens by establishing the household's overall milk consumption and the role of organic within it, then moves to the purchase journey—what triggers a buy, how often, where, and what decides the choice. It then probes product expectations, including certifications and price trade-offs, and closes with satisfaction, loyalty, and switching risk. The arc moves from broad, safe questions about usage to more sensitive topics like price tolerance and switching intent, allowing the segmentation to emerge from behavioural and motivational data.
storyline_notes: Chose price sensitivity + motivation as the lens because organic milk is a premium staple where the key behavioural difference is how much premium buyers will tolerate and what job they hire the milk for (family health, ethics, taste).
Added a 'lactose-free' beat in friction points because the target audience includes lactose-intolerant seekers and the market profile notes dairy-free alternatives as a driver.
Included 'pack size' as a must-cover topic and a beat in product requirements because household size and consumption volume directly affect pack size preferences and price per unit.
The 'willingness to pay' beat is placed late in the product requirements section, as it is the most sensitive item in that tab.
The satisfaction section includes a switching trigger beat that explicitly mentions plant-based alternatives, reflecting the competitive threat from non-dairy options in North America.
The segments are designed to be separable by closed questions on purchase frequency, price sensitivity (via trade-off and willingness-to-pay), and motivations (health vs. ethics vs. taste).
metadata.classification_reason: Household shoppers buy organic milk, pay for it themselves, and decide at the shelf. Retailers and supermarkets sell it, but the end consumer is the individual household. There is no meaningful business-only purchase channel for organic milk.
